topics.title: Pinyin Tones
topics.description: Train your ear for the four tones — the foundation of Mandarin

guide.intro: Mandarin uses pitch to tell words apart. The same syllable in a different tone is a different word — get tones in your ear before you build sentences.

sections.text: Why tones matter
English uses pitch for emotion ("REAL-ly?" vs "really."). Mandarin uses pitch for meaning. "mā" (mom) and "mà" (scold) are not the same word — they're as different as "cat" and "dog".
The four tones + neutral
When you practice, exaggerate. Tones feel embarrassing at first — that's how you know you're doing them right.
Sandhi: tones that shift
Two real-world tweaks: (1) when two 3rd tones meet, the first becomes 2nd: nǐ + hǎo → ní hǎo. (2) 不 (bù) becomes bú before a 4th tone (bú shì). (3) 一 (yī) becomes yí before 4th, yì otherwise.

exercises.prompt: How many tones does Mandarin have (not counting neutral)?
exercises.explanation: Four tones — 1st (flat), 2nd (rising), 3rd (dip), 4th (falling). Plus an unstressed neutral tone.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 1st tone (high and flat)?
exercises.explanation: The macron (¯) over the vowel signals 1st tone — held high and steady.
The acute accent (´) signals 2nd tone — pitch rises like "huh?"

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 3rd tone (dip down then up)?
exercises.explanation: The háček (ˇ) signals 3rd tone — pitch dips then comes back up.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 4th tone (sharp falling)?
exercises.explanation: The grave accent (`) signals 4th tone — short, falling, often emphatic.
媽 is high and flat — the 1st tone. It means "mother."
馬 (horse) dips down then back up — the 3rd tone.
罵 (scold) falls sharply from high to low — the 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "horse" (3rd tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 馬 = mǎ. Use the ˇ mark for 3rd tone (or write "ma3" in numeric pinyin).

exercises.prompt: Mandarin's neutral tone is best described as ___
options: Unstressed and light, often on the second syllable
A 5th tone with its own contour
exercises.answer: Unstressed and light, often on the second syllable
exercises.explanation: Neutral tone has no mark — said quickly, lightly. Common in particles (嗎, 呢) and repeated syllables (媽媽).

exercises.prompt: Which syllable is most likely neutral tone?
exercises.explanation: In doubled family terms like 媽媽, 爸爸, 哥哥 — the second syllable is neutral.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "mother" (1st tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 媽 = mā. First tone, held high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which character matches the 2nd tone (rising) ma-syllable?
exercises.explanation: 麻 (má) is 2nd tone — rising. Means "hemp" or "numb".

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "to scold" (4th tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 罵 = mà. Fourth tone, sharp falling.
麻 (má) — 2nd tone, rising. Means hemp.

exercises.prompt: Two syllables can have the same letters and the same initial — only the ___ makes them different words.
exercises.explanation: Tones are phonemic in Mandarin — they distinguish meaning.
媽 (mā) — flat high tone, means "mother."

exercises.prompt: The mark ¯ over a vowel signals tone number ___
exercises.explanation: The macron (¯) is the 1st tone mark — held high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which tone has the háček (ˇ) mark?
exercises.explanation: The háček ˇ marks 3rd tone — pitch dips then rises.

exercises.prompt: 1st tone is held high and flat. 2nd tone does what?
exercises.explanation: 2nd tone rises from mid to high — same melody as English "huh?"

exercises.prompt: bā vs bá — which one is the 2nd tone?
exercises.explanation: bā 八 (eight) is 1st tone, flat. bá 拔 (to pull) is 2nd tone, rising.

exercises.prompt: fā vs fá — which means "to send / hair" (1st tone)?
exercises.explanation: fā 發 is 1st tone. fá 罰 (to punish) is 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear (1st vs 2nd)
exercises.explanation: 八 (eight) is flat and high — the 1st tone.
十 (ten) rises — the 2nd tone. Don't confuse with 是 shì (is, 4th tone).
發 fā is held flat and high.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin (with tone mark) for "ten":
exercises.explanation: 十 = shí — rising tone. Compare with shī 失 (to lose), which is flat.
Mid → high, all one smooth rise. Borrow your English question intonation.
拔 (to pull out) is 2nd tone, rising.
1st tone is held high and steady, like singing one note.
八 bā — flat first tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 拔 ("to pull"):
exercises.explanation: 拔 bá — rising second tone.
十 shí — 2nd tone, rising.
失 shī (lose) — first tone, flat.

exercises.prompt: Which is the 1st-tone partner to 拔 (bá)?
exercises.explanation: 八 bā (8) — same syllable as 拔 bá but 1st tone instead of 2nd.

exercises.prompt: To produce the 2nd tone, your voice should ___
Type the pinyin for the 1st-tone partner of fá ("punish"):
exercises.explanation: 發 fā — flat 1st tone. 罰 fá — rising 2nd tone.
Rising 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: Which English melody resembles Mandarin's 2nd tone?

options: Dips down then comes back up
exercises.answer: Dips down then comes back up
exercises.explanation: Mid → low → mid. In careful speech the dip is dramatic; in quick speech it's often a low "half-3rd".

exercises.prompt: mǎi vs mài — which means "to buy"?
exercises.explanation: 買 mǎi = buy (dipping). 賣 mài = sell (falling). Remember: 賣 has the extra 十 on top — "goods piled up to sell."

exercises.prompt: kàn means "to look/watch." What tone is it?
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — sharp falling. (kǎn 砍 "to chop" with 3rd tone is a different word.)
買 dips and rises — 3rd tone.
賣 falls sharply — 4th tone.
看 kàn — sharp, falling 4th tone.
那 nà = that — 4th tone. Compare 哪 nǎ = which — 3rd tone.
看 kàn — 4th tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: You hear a single short, falling syllable. What tone is it most likely?
exercises.explanation: Short + falling = 4th. Native speakers often shorten 4th tone in casual speech.

options: Sharp falling from high to low
exercises.answer: Sharp falling from high to low
exercises.explanation: 4th tone is the dramatic crash — high to low, abrupt.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 賣 ("to sell"):
exercises.explanation: 賣 mài — 4th tone, sharp falling.
那 nà — 4th tone, falling.
買 mǎi — 3rd tone, dipping.
哪 nǎ — 3rd tone, dipping.

exercises.prompt: The pair 買 / 賣 differs by ___
exercises.explanation: Same initial m + ai. Tones change meaning entirely.

exercises.prompt: Which tone is often shortened in fast speech?
Order tones from 1 to 4 using the standard ma-syllable
exercises.answer: 媽 麻 馬 罵
exercises.explanation: 媽 (1st) → 麻 (2nd) → 馬 (3rd) → 罵 (4th). The classic teaching set.
看 kàn — 4th tone.
Sharp falling — 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: What happens when two 3rd tones meet (3rd-tone sandhi)?
exercises.explanation: 3 + 3 → 2 + 3. So nǐ + hǎo is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo.

exercises.prompt: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo. What does it sound like?
exercises.explanation: First 3rd tone shifts to 2nd. Pinyin keeps the original marks; your mouth does the shift.

exercises.prompt: 很好 (hěn hǎo, "very good") — what does it sound like?
exercises.explanation: Two 3rd tones in a row → first becomes 2nd. Said hén hǎo.
你好 — the most common hello. Note the sandhi: written nǐ hǎo, said ní hǎo.
很好 — said hén hǎo because of 3rd-tone sandhi.

exercises.prompt: How is sandhi written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: Standard convention: write nǐ hǎo, say ní hǎo. The shift is in your mouth, not on the page.

exercises.prompt: Three 3rd tones in 我也好 (wǒ yě hǎo, "I'm also good"). The first two shift. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Chains of 3rd tones: most become 2nd, only the last stays 3rd. wǒ yě hǎo → wó yé hǎo.
可以 ("can / may") — written kě yǐ, said ké yǐ (sandhi).

exercises.prompt: Does sandhi apply across pauses/sentence breaks?
options: Always, every time two 3rd tones touch
Only within a single word or tight phrase
exercises.answer: Only within a single word or tight phrase
exercises.explanation: Sandhi follows the rhythm of the phrase. If you'd naturally pause between the syllables, no shift.
3+3 → 2+3. Written marks stay; the change is spoken.

exercises.prompt: How is 很好 actually pronounced?
exercises.explanation: 3+3 → 2+3. Written hěn hǎo, spoken hén hǎo.
Only when two 3rd tones touch within a phrase.
可以 — written kě yǐ, said ké yǐ (sandhi).

options: Mental — not shown on the page
exercises.answer: Mental — not shown on the page
exercises.explanation: Standard convention keeps the original 3rd-tone marks. The shift lives in the mouth.

exercises.prompt: Three 3rd tones — only the LAST stays 3rd. Type the spoken version of 我也好:
exercises.explanation: Chains shift: most syllables become 2nd, only the last keeps 3rd.

exercises.prompt: Does sandhi apply across a pause/comma?

exercises.explanation: 我很好 with 3-3 sandhi: wó hěn hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT affected by 3-3 sandhi?
exercises.explanation: 明天 mingtiān — 2nd + 1st. No two 3rd tones to clash.

lessons.title: 不 and 一 sandhi
lessons.description: When bù becomes bú and yī becomes yí/yì

exercises.prompt: 不 (bù) means "not." What's its default tone?
exercises.explanation: 不 is normally 4th tone — bù. It only shifts before another 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: 不 + 是 (shì, "is") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 becomes 2nd: bú shì "is not."

exercises.prompt: 不 + 來 (lái, 2nd tone, "come") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before any non-4th tone, 不 stays 4th: bù lái "not come."

exercises.prompt: 一 (yī) means "one." Before a 4th tone like 個 (gè), it becomes...
exercises.explanation: 一 + 4th → yí. So 一個 is yí ge in speech.

exercises.prompt: 一 + 起 (qǐ, 3rd tone, "rise") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before non-4th tones (1st, 2nd, 3rd), 一 becomes 4th: yì qǐ "together."
不是 — 不 shifts to 2nd tone before 是 (4th).
一個 = yí ge — one (thing). 個 is neutral in speech but counts as 4th for sandhi.
一起 = yì qǐ — together. 一 became 4th before 3rd-tone 起.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不 + 要 (yào, 4th, "want") in speech?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 becomes 2nd: bú yào "don't want / don't."

exercises.prompt: When does 一 NOT shift tone?
options: When standing alone or saying numbers in sequence
exercises.answer: When standing alone or saying numbers in sequence
exercises.explanation: Counting (yī, èr, sān...) or year numbers (一九九九) keeps 一 as 1st tone. Sandhi only kicks in when 一 leads into another syllable as part of a meaning unit.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不 + 對 (duì, 4th, "correct")?
exercises.explanation: Before 4th tone, 不 shifts to 2nd: bú duì.

exercises.prompt: Before any non-4th tone, 不 stays ___
exercises.explanation: 不 + 1st/2nd/3rd → bù (4th, unchanged). Only 不 + 4th → bú.
Before non-4th tones, 一 shifts to 4th: yì tiān.

exercises.prompt: How is 一年 (one year) spoken?
exercises.explanation: 一 + 2nd (年 nián) → 一 becomes 4th: yì nián.
不 + 2nd-tone 來 → unchanged: bù lái.

exercises.prompt: 不 changes tone only when followed by ___
exercises.explanation: Sandhi rule for 不: only before 4th tones does it shift to 2nd.

exercises.prompt: How is 一千 (one thousand) spoken?
exercises.explanation: 一 + 1st (千 qiān) → 一 becomes 4th.
Before 4th tone 要, 不 → bú.

exercises.prompt: In counting (yī, èr, sān…) what tone does 一 keep?
exercises.explanation: Sandhi doesn't apply when 一 is standing alone or counting.

exercises.prompt: Order: bú shì → before this 4th-tone character, 不 shifts to 2nd

topics.title: Pinyin Sounds
topics.description: The tricky consonants and vowels of pinyin — the ones English doesn't have

guide.intro: Pinyin is the romanization that lets you type, look up, and pronounce Mandarin. Most letters do what you'd expect — but a handful are traps for English speakers.

sections.text: Initials: where sound starts
Mandarin has three pairs that English speakers mix up: zh/ch/sh (retroflex — curl your tongue back) vs z/c/s (sibilant — tongue flat). Plus j/q/x — like Italian's c/g — always followed by i or ü.

rows: j in 'jar' with tongue curled back

sections.text: j / q / x — the i/ü trio
j, q, x are softer than zh, ch, sh — tongue stays forward. They only ever appear before i or ü. After j/q/x, ü is written as plain u (so 居 is jū, but the vowel is really ü).
qù sounds like "chü" — NOT "q-you" or "tsoo." The q is a soft "ch" and ù is a rounded "ee" with pursed lips.
Finals: the trap vowels
Some finals don't match their spelling. -ian sounds like "yen," not "yan." -uan after j/q/x/y is really -üan (so 元 yuán = "yu-en"). -eng has a back "ung" feel vs -en which is light and forward.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between zh and z?
options: zh is retroflex (tongue curls back); z is flat
z is retroflex; zh is flat
exercises.answer: zh is retroflex (tongue curls back); z is flat
exercises.explanation: zh/ch/sh = tongue curled back (retroflex). z/c/s = tongue flat. Easy to mix up; speakers in southern China often merge them.

exercises.prompt: 知 ("to know") is zhī. How is 資 ("resource") spelled?
exercises.explanation: 知 zhī uses the retroflex zh; 資 zī uses flat z. Same vowel, different tongue position.

exercises.prompt: Which English sound is closest to Mandarin c (as in 詞 cí)?
exercises.explanation: c is the "ts" cluster — no h, no curl. Don't read it as English "c."

exercises.prompt: 吃 ("to eat") is chī. How is 詞 ("word") spelled?
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī uses retroflex ch; 詞 cí uses flat c. Common minimal pair.
Retroflex zh — tongue curled back.
四 sì — flat s, no tongue curl, 4th tone.
是 shì — retroflex sh, tongue curls back.
是 shì — retroflex sh, 4th tone. The most common verb "to be."

exercises.prompt: Which is a fact about southern-China accents?
options: They distinguish zh/z more carefully than the north
They often merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s
exercises.answer: They often merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s
exercises.explanation: Many southern speakers (Shanghai, Taiwan, etc.) don't distinguish retroflex from flat — they pronounce 是 closer to sì. Standard Mandarin (北京話) keeps them apart.

exercises.prompt: Which sound requires tongue curled back?
exercises.explanation: zh/ch/sh are retroflex — tongue tip curls back.

exercises.prompt: Which is the flat sibilant partner of sh?
exercises.explanation: s is the flat partner; sh is retroflex.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 吃 ("to eat"):
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī — retroflex ch, 1st tone.
詞 cí — flat c, 2nd tone.
私 sī — flat s, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Native speakers from which region most consistently distinguish zh/z?
exercises.explanation: Northern Mandarin (Beijing) keeps retroflex distinct from flat.
吃 chī — retroflex ch.

exercises.prompt: c in Mandarin pinyin sounds like ___
exercises.explanation: c = ts, never English c. No aspiration mistake.
資 zī — flat z, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 知 ("to know"):
exercises.explanation: 知 zhī — retroflex zh, 1st tone.

lessons.title: Tricky j/q/x + i/ü
lessons.description: When 'u' is really 'ü' and q isn't English q

exercises.prompt: j, q, x can ONLY be followed by which vowels?
exercises.explanation: Hard rule: j/q/x never appear before a, o, u, e by themselves. They only pair with i (as in ji, qi, xi) or ü (written u, as in ju, qu, xu).

exercises.prompt: 居 is spelled "jū." What's the actual vowel sound?
options: ü (rounded ee — say ee with pursed lips)
exercises.answer: ü (rounded ee — say ee with pursed lips)
exercises.explanation: After j/q/x/y, ü drops its dots: jū looks like "ju" but is really jü. Make ee with rounded lips.

exercises.prompt: 去 ("to go") is qù. How would you describe the sound?
exercises.explanation: q is a soft, forward "ch" — not the English q. ù is the rounded-ee. So qù is more like "chü" than anything in English.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is actually pronounced with ü?
exercises.explanation: ju, qu, xu, yu are all really jü, qü, xü, yü. zhu, chu, shu, zu, cu, su use real u.

exercises.prompt: What does the x in Mandarin sound like?
options: soft sh — tongue forward, like a German "ich" softened
exercises.answer: soft sh — tongue forward, like a German "ich" softened
exercises.explanation: x = a forward, light "sh." Tongue near the roof of the mouth, no curling. 謝 xiè ("thanks") and 學 xué are common.
qù — soft ch + ü, 4th tone.
xué — soft x + ü-e diphthong, 2nd tone (rising). "To study/learn."
jī — soft j (like "jee"), 1st tone. Don't confuse with retroflex zhī.
xué — that x is the soft, forward "sh," and ue is really üe.

exercises.prompt: Why is the ü written as plain u after j, q, x, y?
options: Because they can never take real u anyway, so no ambiguity
It's actually pronounced as u in those cases
exercises.answer: Because they can never take real u anyway, so no ambiguity
exercises.explanation: Since j/q/x/y never pair with the back-u sound, the system drops the dots — "ju" can only mean jü, so writing it that way saves keystrokes.

exercises.prompt: After which initials does the umlaut on ü drop in writing?
exercises.explanation: j/q/x/y can only pair with ü, never u — so no ambiguity, dots dropped.
雞 jī — soft j + i, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 去 ("to go"):
exercises.explanation: 去 qù — soft ch + ü, 4th tone.
雪 xuě — soft x + üe, 3rd tone, means snow.

exercises.prompt: How do you pronounce j in Mandarin?
options: Soft, like English 'j' but lighter and forward
exercises.answer: Soft, like English 'j' but lighter and forward

exercises.prompt: Which syllable contains a real ü sound (rounded ee)?
exercises.explanation: qu is qü; chu/zhu/ku take the back u.
西 xī — soft x + i, 1st tone.
學 xué — "to study/learn."
雞 jī — soft j + i.

exercises.prompt: To make the ü vowel, you should ___
見 is jiàn. How does -ian sound?
exercises.explanation: -ian doesn't sound like its spelling. jiàn rhymes with English "yen," not "yawn."
Trust the sound, not the spelling. jian = jyen, mian = myen, tian = tyen.

exercises.prompt: 元 is yuán. What's the actual sound?
exercises.explanation: After y, the uan is really üan, which sounds like the ü of jü followed by -en. yuán = "yü-en."

exercises.prompt: 聽 tīng vs 真 zhēn — what's the final difference?
exercises.explanation: -eng/-ing are deep, back nasal (like English 'ung'). -en/-in are light, forward (like English 'en').

exercises.prompt: Which is correct for 聽 ("to listen")?
exercises.explanation: 聽 is tīng — 1st tone, -ing final (back nasal).
見 jiàn — "jyen" with 4th tone.
yuán — "yü-en," rising tone. All four options share this pronunciation; 元 is the currency unit.
聽 tīng — flat 1st tone with back nasal -ing.
zhēn — retroflex zh + light forward -en + 1st tone. Compare 真 zhēn (real) vs 正 zhèng (right/correct, with -eng).
Compare 元 yuán (yü-en) with 關 guān (gwan). Same letters, different vowel because of the preceding initial.
jiàn rhymes with English yen, not yawn.

exercises.prompt: The final -uan after g/k/h sounds like ___
exercises.explanation: 關 guān = gwan. Different from yuán (yü-en).

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 見 ("to see"):
exercises.explanation: 見 jiàn — "jyen" with 4th tone.
元 yuán — "yü-en," 2nd tone.
停 tíng (stop) — 2nd tone, -ing final.

options: -en is a back nasal, -eng is forward
-en is forward, -eng is a back nasal
exercises.answer: -en is forward, -eng is a back nasal

exercises.explanation: 聽 tīng — 1st tone, -ing final.
面 miàn — "myen" with 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Compare 真 (zhēn) vs 正 (zhèng) — what's the final difference?
exercises.explanation: 真 forward -en. 正 back -eng.
Trust the sound, not the spelling: -ian = yen.

exercises.prompt: 你 = nǐ. What two pinyin pieces does it have?
exercises.explanation: Initial n + final i + tone mark = nǐ. The two-piece structure is the universal pinyin recipe.

options: All — depending on how you write tones
exercises.answer: All — depending on how you write tones
exercises.explanation: All three appear in the wild: nǐ hǎo (formal pinyin), ní hǎo (spoken sandhi notation, less common), ni hao (no tones, informal/SMS). Beginner standard is nǐ hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Read this pinyin: "wǒ shì xuéshēng." What does it mean?
exercises.explanation: wǒ (I) + shì (am) + xuéshēng (student) = 我是學生.
中國 zhōngguó — "middle kingdom." Retroflex zh + back -ong + g- + -uo.
謝謝 xièxie — repeated x sounds. Second syllable is neutral tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap the character that matches what you hear
exercises.explanation: 我 wǒ — initial w + o final + 3rd tone.
中國 — two retroflex+back syllables. Listen for the deep 'ong' nasal.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin (with tones) for 謝謝 ("thank you"):
exercises.explanation: 謝謝 xièxie — the second is neutral. Two soft x sounds.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin (with tones) for 中國 ("China"):
exercises.explanation: zhōngguó — 1st tone + 2nd tone. Retroflex zh on syllable 1.

topics.title: How Characters Work
topics.description: Chinese characters are made of reusable pieces — learn to spot them

guide.intro: Chinese characters look intimidating but they're built from a small set of reusable pieces. Once you see the pattern, learning new characters speeds up.

sections.text: Characters are made of pieces

Almost every Chinese character is a combination of smaller components. Some components are simple characters in their own right; others (radicals) only appear as parts of larger characters. Recognizing the pieces makes the whole easier.

rows.translation: rest (a person leaning on a tree)

sections.text: Radicals as meaning clues

About 200 "radicals" group characters by meaning. If a character contains 氵 (water), it likely relates to water (rivers, drinking, thirst). 心 (heart) → emotions. 口 (mouth) → speech and eating. The radical doesn't tell you the whole meaning, but it points you in the right neighborhood.

topics.title: Greetings
topics.description: Say hello, goodbye, and how are you

guide.intro: Mandarin has only a handful of greetings to learn — but the tones really matter. Here's what to know before you start.

sections.text: The four tones

Every Mandarin syllable has one of four pitched tones (plus a neutral "fifth" tone). The same syllable means different things depending on tone — so "mā", "má", "mǎ", and "mà" are four different words.
Hello: 你好 (nǐ hǎo)
你 means "you" and 好 means "good". Put them together for "you good?" — the standard hello, usable any time of day.
When two 3rd-tone syllables stack like nǐ hǎo, the first one shifts up to a 2nd tone in speech (ní hǎo). It still gets written as nǐ hǎo.
你 (nǐ) vs 您 (nín)
您 is the polite form of "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers. 你 is everyday/casual. Both pronounced almost the same.
How are you?
To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just add 嗎 (ma) at the end. So 你好 ("you're good") + 嗎 = 你好嗎? ("are you good?").

topics.description: Count, ask how many, give your age

guide.intro: Mandarin numbers are wonderfully regular — once you know 1 to 10 and the word for "ten", you can build every number up to 99.

sections.text: One to ten
Building 11–99
After ten, numbers are built like math problems. Read characters left to right, multiplying anything before 十 and adding anything after.
Same trick goes further: 一百 (one hundred), 一千 (one thousand), 一萬 (ten thousand) — but Chinese groups large numbers in 萬 (10,000) rather than thousands.
Two: 二 vs 兩
Mandarin has two words for "two". 二 (èr) is the digit — used in counting, math, and phone numbers. 兩 (liǎng) means "a pair of" — used before measure words and quantities.
Asking how many

guide.intro: Mandarin has no verb conjugation, no plural endings, no genders, and no articles. Once you know the word order, the language gets out of your way.

sections.text: Word order: subject – verb – object
Just like English, a basic sentence puts the subject first, the verb second, and the object last.
Pronouns are simple
他 (he) and 她 (she) are pronounced exactly the same — only the writing changes. In speech, listeners use context.
The verb 是 (shì)
是 means "to be" — but only for nouns connecting to other nouns ("I am a student"). For adjectives, you don't use 是; you use 很 (hěn) instead, which means "very" but is often a placeholder.
Negation: 不 vs 沒
Use 不 (bù) for negating present and future actions, and for adjectives. Use 沒 (méi) for past actions and for the verb 有 ("to have").

sections.text: No tenses!
Mandarin verbs do not change form for past, present, or future. Time is shown by adding a time word (yesterday, tomorrow) or particles like 了 (le) for completion.

topics.title: Common verbs
topics.description: Go, eat, want, like, see, listen

guide.intro: Mandarin verbs never change form. The same character is used for all persons and all times — context (and time words) does the heavy lifting.

sections.text: One verb, every form
Compare with English: "go / goes / went / will go" — Mandarin uses 去 for all of them. The action stays put; you add words around it.
Want vs. would-like: 要 / 想 / 喜歡
These three look interchangeable in English but have a clear pecking order in Mandarin.

rows: I want / I will (decisive, ordering food)
I would like / I am thinking about

rows.source: 我 想 喝 咖啡。
rows.translation: I would like to drink coffee.

sections.text: Completion: the 了 particle
Adding 了 (le) after a verb signals an action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to past tense — but it's really an aspect marker, not a tense.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 飯。

sections.text: Don't sprinkle 了 everywhere — for adjectives ("I am happy") or stative verbs, you don't use it. Save it for completed actions.

guide.intro: Time words go at the start of a sentence or right after the subject — never at the end like English. "Tomorrow I go" is the natural Mandarin order.

sections.text: Days are math
Days of the week are 星期 (xīngqī, "week") + the digit. So 星期一 is week-1 (Monday), 星期二 is week-2 (Tuesday), and so on through 星期六. Sunday is the odd one out: 星期天 or 星期日.
Telling time
Hours use 點 (diǎn, "o'clock"), minutes use 分 (fēn). Half-past is 半 (bàn). "Quarter" is 一刻 (yí kè) for :15 and 三刻 for :45.
